stories.title: Singapore's Air Turns Unhealthy in Every Corner
stories.headline_kid: For the first time since 2019, the air quality in every part of Singapore turned unhealthy today because of haze.
summary: Early on Tuesday morning, Singapore's air quality dropped into the 'unhealthy' range in all five regions of the island — north, south, east, west and central. The central area was the worst, with its 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reaching 154. This is the first time since September 2019 that every single region has been unhealthy at the same time.

The haze is caused by smoke from fires burning in nearby countries. Strong winds carry the smoke particles across the sea until they settle over Singapore, making the sky look grey and blurry, like a photo taken through a dusty window.

Because breathing in hazy air isn't good for our lungs, many people are wearing masks outdoors, and some schools may cut down on outdoor sports or move activities indoors. People with asthma or breathing problems, as well as very young children and the elderly, need to be extra careful.

The National Environment Agency (NEA) is watching the situation closely and will update the public if things get better or worse. Everyone is hoping the wind direction changes soon to blow the smoke away.

lenses.me: Your outdoor PE lesson or CCA training might be cancelled or moved indoors if the haze stays bad.
lenses.family: Your family might change weekend plans, avoid the park, and keep masks ready at home just in case.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates might need to stay indoors during recess instead of playing outside.
lenses.nation: Singapore hasn't seen haze this bad across the whole country since 2019, so the government is monitoring the air very closely.
lenses.world: The haze shows how fires in one country can affect the health of people living far away in another country.

stories.title: A Year On: Family Still Seeks Answers for Singaporean Coach
stories.headline_kid: A year after a Singaporean cricket coach passed away while working in Africa, his family is still waiting to learn what really happened.
summary: Mr Arjun Menon was a Singaporean who worked as a cricket coach in Malawi, a country in Africa, teaching children and helping to grow the sport there. Sadly, he passed away at his home in Malawi in May last year.

More than a year later, his sister, Ms Prema Menon, says the family still does not have full answers about what happened. She has been trying to get updates from the authorities in Malawi but says the family feels left in the dark.

Because Mr Menon died overseas, the investigation is being carried out by police in Malawi, not Singapore. The Singapore government has been providing support to the family, but solving crimes across two different countries can take a long time and be very difficult.
Ms Menon says her brother loved coaching and cared deeply about the children he taught. The family continues to hope that one day they will finally learn the truth and find some closure.

lenses.me: It reminds us how important it is to know that loved ones working far from home are safe.
lenses.family: Imagine how hard it would be if someone in your family was working far away and something happened — it shows how strong family love and hope can be.
lenses.friends: You could talk with friends about how sports like cricket can connect people from different countries.
lenses.nation: It shows how the Singapore government supports citizens and their families when tragic things happen overseas.
lenses.world: It shows that getting justice across different countries can be slow, and nations often need to work together to help families get answers.

stories.title: Singapore Hosts Big Sea Dispute Between Thailand and Cambodia
stories.headline_kid: Cambodia and Thailand are asking a panel of international judges — meeting right here in Singapore — to help settle their disagreement over the sea between them.
summary: Cambodia and Thailand have been disagreeing about which country owns which part of the sea in the Gulf of Thailand. This matters a lot because the area may have oil and gas hidden under the seabed, which both countries would like to use.

In 2001, the two countries had agreed to share and explore the area together, but Thailand later pulled out of that agreement. Cambodia then asked a United Nations-backed panel called the Permanent Court of Arbitration to step in and help solve the disagreement fairly.

This important hearing is taking place in Singapore. Singapore is often chosen by countries around the world as a trusted, neutral place to hold talks and settle disputes — a bit like choosing a fair referee that both teams trust.
No one knows yet how the dispute will end, but the world is watching closely to see if it can be solved peacefully through talking, instead of through conflict.

lenses.nation: It highlights Singapore's reputation as a fair, neutral place where countries feel safe discussing their problems.
lenses.world: Solving disputes over resources peacefully, instead of through conflict, helps keep countries and their people safe.

stories.title: Why Sugar Prices in India Could Affect Your Deepavali Sweets
stories.headline_kid: Sugar prices have shot up in India just as families prepare to buy sweet treats for the festival of Deepavali.
summary: Deepavali, the festival of lights, is coming up in November, and many families love to buy or make sweet treats to celebrate. But in India, sugar prices have risen a lot recently, making these festive sweets more expensive to produce.

Prices have come down slightly from their highest point, but they are still much higher than usual. This is a bit like when there's less of a toy you want in stock — shops end up charging more for it because it's harder to get.

The Indian government is now trying to control sugar prices before demand shoots up even more closer to Deepavali. Sweet shop owners are worried that higher costs will eat into their profits, and some families may need to budget more carefully for festive shopping.

This matters here too because Singapore has a big Indian community that celebrates Deepavali. Shops in areas like Little India that sell traditional sweets may also see prices rise slightly, since sugar and ingredient costs are often connected across countries.

lenses.family: Parents may need to plan and budget more carefully for festive shopping this year.
lenses.friends: Friends who celebrate Deepavali can chat about how festive treats and traditions might be affected.
lenses.nation: Singapore's Little India shops and shoppers are connected to price changes happening in other countries.
lenses.world: It shows how the price of one simple ingredient, like sugar, can affect people's celebrations in many countries at once.

stories.title: From Pain to Purpose: Injured Worker Builds a School for Kids
stories.headline_kid: Ten years after being badly hurt in a workplace accident in Singapore, a former migrant worker used his compensation money to build a school in Bangladesh — and now he's making it even bigger.
summary: Mohammad Ataur Rahman came to Singapore to work, but ten years ago he was badly burned in a workplace explosion. It was a painful and scary time for him, and he needed a long time to recover.

In Singapore, injured workers can receive compensation, which is money given to help them while they recover or cannot work. Instead of only using the money for himself, Mr Rahman used part of it to build a school in his hometown in Bangladesh, called Al-Shohag school.
A decade later, his small act of kindness has grown into something much bigger. He is now expanding the school so that even more children in his community can get a good education.

Mr Rahman's story shows how something painful can be turned into something that helps many others. It's also a reminder of how important it is for workplaces to look after and protect workers who come from other countries to work in Singapore.
